segments.text: Hello everyone. Let's go over the spring list: Inès Delorme's debut novel, the essay translated from Italian and the photo book on Breton lighthouses. All three reach bookshops in the second week of March. There's a lot to cover, so let's be quick.
Before we start, the printer has confirmed his lead time: three weeks between sign-off and delivery.
On production, the novel runs to two hundred and eighty pages. For the print run, I suggest three thousand copies: that's the threshold where the unit cost falls below two euros.
The sales reps are confident, the novel went down well at the launch meeting. Three thousand suits me.
Three thousand for me too.
Understood, we're going ahead with a first print run of three thousand copies for the novel.
For the paper, the printer is offering an ivory bulky stock at eighty grams, the same as for last year's novel.
Benoît, can you also ask him for a quote on an equivalent recycled paper? I'd like to compare, as long as we stay within the forty-two thousand euro production budget.
Sure, I'll ask him for the quote tomorrow.
On the press side, I'll send you the full press kit, including the author interview, by Wednesday.
Very good, two regional radio stations have already asked for copies. Nora, for the booksellers' presentation evening in early December, can you book the room at Les Rives bookshop?
Will do, I'll call the bookshop tomorrow to block a date.
For the sales reps, I'll prepare a selling sheet on the three titles by Friday, for their sales meeting.
And the author's bookshop tour, I'll organize it: about ten dates between March and April, mostly in Brittany and Paris.
For the photo book, I'll order the colour proofs from the printer and follow them through to sign-off.
The photo book is still our biggest risk: a hundred and twenty pages in full colour, selling at twenty-nine euros.
Perfect. Another point: the rights to the book's three archive photos still haven't been checked, and that has to be sorted before sign-off.
For the essay, Pascale, our translator, will take care of proofreading the translation.
The essay runs to a hundred and ninety pages, and the translation is eighty percent done.
Loïc, could you contact the Geneva book fair to get us a panel on the essay?
Not for now, with the winter fairs I'm swamped. Let's move on.
Pity, Geneva worked well for us two years ago.
Benoît, that idea of a paperback edition of last year's novel, have you had a chance to look at it?
Not yet. I could cost it out if the printer gets back to me quickly, but no promises.
For the covers, I propose all three titles follow the new graphic guidelines, with the colour band at the bottom.
Yes, the new guidelines for all three, booksellers will recognize the house.
Fine by me, even though the band costs two cents more per copy.
Adopted: all three covers follow the new guidelines.
Personally, I'm dropping phone follow-ups with journalists, I'll only use email from now on. It suits me better.
What about an audiobook of the novel? Several booksellers have mentioned it to me.
It's tempting, but not for this spring. We'll set the idea aside until next autumn.
We're still missing the back cover text for the photo book.
Who can write it?
Well, since nobody's stepping up, I'll do it: I'll write it for Monday.
Thanks. Careful, the series limits the back cover to twelve hundred characters.
A word on pre-orders: the distributor reports six hundred and forty copies for the novel, half of what we expected. The essay is at four hundred, which is in line.
Not all the independent bookshops have answered yet, but it won't double.
That will weigh on the print run, we'll have to come back to it.
Yes. Benoît, by the way, forget the recycled paper quote, I no longer need it: the printer only has one in stock and it's too thin.
Fine, I won't ask for it.
A small change on the press kit: on Wednesday, I'll only send the press release, without the interview. The author is only available for the interview the following week.
Actually, with so few pre-orders, the room at Les Rives bookshop is becoming unnecessary, don't you think?
I agree with Loïc, an evening event is a lot for that figure.
Let's move on to the novel's print run, as it happens.

With six hundred and forty pre-orders, three thousand copies is too risky. I suggest we revisit our earlier choice and print two thousand, with a quick reprint if it sells well. A reprint of a thousand copies takes ten days at our printer.
I agree, two thousand.
Two thousand works for me too.
Then we drop the three thousand: first print run of two thousand copies, reprint if needed. That's agreed for everyone.
Something else: the selling sheet for the reps, don't count on me after all. The distributor is doing one on their side, I won't prepare it.
I have a problem too: the bookshop tour, I can't organize it on top of the press work. Loïc, would you be up for handling it instead of me? You know the booksellers better than I do.
OK, the tour is mine from now on. I'll send you a calendar of the dates by the end of the month.
As for the colour proofs for the photo book, I'd happily hand them to Nora, if she wants to deal with them.
Last point, the schedule: the novel's signed-off proof must go to the printer by November 12 at the latest. Benoît, will you make sure of that?
Yes, I'll make sure: the signed-off proof will go out on November 12.
That leaves four months before release, we're on schedule.
Thanks, everyone. We'll meet again in two weeks.
